DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Spring 2026 Menu Pricing Review

## Bottom line

I wouldn't approve this as written. The price increases may well be reasonable, but the £42k headline is overstated, and the risotto recommendation contradicts the paper's own Table 1. The author's description ("low-risk, well evidenced, easy improvement") is stronger than the document supports.

## What holds up

- The Table 1 margins and plate totals are internally consistent (1,050 plates).
- The £810/week and £42,120/year figures are correct arithmetic *if* volumes and costs stay flat and the restaurant trades 52 full weeks.
- The competitor ranges and the "below the midpoint" claims are accurate: £17.50 vs £17.98, £16.00 vs £16.50, £28.00 vs £29.50.
- Raising prices when costs have outpaced them is a sensible direction.

## Main problems

**1. The risotto rationale is factually wrong.** Risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest. Steak is the lowest at 60%. At £11.20 gross profit per plate, risotto earns more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90). It is the lowest seller among named dishes, but that is the only part of the claim that is true.

Replacing it is not "an easy improvement." The paper's own specials line runs at 64%. If the new special at £14 performs like that and sells 90 a week, gross profit falls by about £200 a week (roughly £10.5k a year), around a quarter of the claimed gain. The risotto may also be the only vegetarian main, and the paper doesn't say whether the replacement is costed.

**2. The 12% beef increase is in the supplier section but not in the projection.** Beef affects the steak and (mostly) the burger. If most of the plate cost is beef, that is roughly +£1.25 per steak and +£0.30 to £0.50 per burger. That comes to about £230 to £280 a week, which erodes a third of the £810. The steak margin ends up near 58% even at £28. The price rises mainly offset cost inflation. They don't add £42k on top of today's profit.

**3. The margin claim doesn't survive the other proposals.** My estimate is that mains margin is currently about 69 to 70% (it depends on specials pricing, which isn't given). The price rises alone take it to roughly 70 to 71%, so the paper's 71% is fair in isolation. Add the beef increase and a 64% special in place of risotto, and it falls to roughly 68%, *below* today. Net of both, the gain is closer to £350 a week (about £17k to £20k a year) than £810.

The paper also frames this as restoring a 70% *overall* target. Mains are already near 70%, so the slide from 70% to 67% must come mainly from the other courses, which the paper doesn't examine.

**4. "Volumes will hold" is an assumption, not evidence.**
- There is no sensitivity analysis. Rough break-even is a loss of about 60 plates a week (~9% of the 690 repriced plates), before counting lost drinks and starter spend.
- Repeat guests are the ones who know the old prices, so a 60% repeat share doesn't demonstrate low price sensitivity. It is also a share of bookings, not covers.
- The 2024 precedent is based on bookings only, 18 months old, and the paper gives no information on the size of that change.
- Increases of 6% (fish), 7% (burger) and 8% (steak) are more than "a pound or two" implies.

**5. The "value option" claim is weaker than stated.** We are currently cheapest on all three dishes. After the rises we'd be above the cheapest competitor on each (£17.50 vs £16.95, £16.00 vs £15.50, £28.00 vs £27.00). A range midpoint isn't a typical price, and five competitors and three dishes is a thin benchmark. Curry and risotto weren't benchmarked at all.

**6. Errors and weak data foundations.**
- Section 8 says "six trading days a week," but Wed to Sun is five.
- The baseline is two winter months. Spring volumes and mix may differ, so the January/February comparison will confuse seasonality with price effects.
- "Weekday lunch is a small share" is asserted without a figure.

**7. The monitoring plan is thin.** It has no trigger thresholds, no decision-maker or fallback, and tracks plates only, not covers, bookings or spend per head. With menus reprinted on 1 April, reversing a change is slow. Use last year's March to May as the comparator if available, and define in advance what drop triggers a review.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. Rebuild the projection with the beef increase, per-dish beef share of cost, and a specials-based cost for the risotto replacement.
2. Keep the risotto, or justify its removal on grounds other than margin (kitchen complexity, waste, strategic fit). Check the vegetarian offer.
3. Add a volume sensitivity (for example -5%, -10%, -15%) and show break-even.
4. Fix the trading-days error and state the 52-week assumption.
5. Reconsider the steak and burger moves in light of beef costs. Consider whether the curry, with its low cost and high margin, deserves a look.
6. Examine starters, desserts and any other courses, since that is where the margin slide appears to be.
7. Set explicit review triggers for the eight-week monitoring.
